narrativeReportMd:
# ObservationDefinition R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking changes were found. `ObservationDefinition` keeps the same canonical identity, but R6 remodels the resource from a compact R4 definition into a more canonical publication artifact with required `status`, new metadata, new observation-context capabilities, replacement of `quantitativeDetails`, and restructuring of qualified intervals and coded value sets.

## Scope
The analysis used the R4 and R6 core StructureDefinitions, package metadata, package index entries, the assignment manifest, and relevant local ValueSet/CodeSystem files. Inherited base-resource and datatype changes are out of scope.

## Main migration themes
The most important R4-to-R6 validation break is the new mandatory modifier `ObservationDefinition.status`. Existing R4 instances also break when they use removed local paths such as `quantitativeDetails`, `qualifiedInterval`, or top-level coded value set references. The largest R6-to-R4 risk is that R6 can express canonical metadata, derivation, subject/performer/specimen/device/group/component structure, context-specific qualified values, and canonical ValueSet links that R4 has no native fields for.

## Highest-impact findings
High-impact findings are the mandatory `status`, the replacement of `quantitativeDetails` by `permittedUnit`, the `qualifiedInterval` to `qualifiedValue` restructure, and the move/type change for valid/normal/abnormal/critical coded value sets.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important where R4 data must be mapped losslessly: SI/customary unit details, conversion factor, decimal precision, old top-level ValueSet References, and gender-to-sex-parameter semantics need local policy decisions.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several R6 changes could have been modeled less disruptively by keeping deprecated R4 elements alongside new elements for one release or by using optional extensions. The R6 model appears to favor a cleaner canonical-definition model and richer Observation semantics over direct wire compatibility.

## Follow-up analysis
Review base resource/datatype reports separately, and use official terminology services for LOINC, SNOMED CT, and UCUM before making final terminology migration policy.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `ObservationDefinition` has material local breaking changes between R4 and R6. The top migration concerns are the new required modifier `status`, removal/replacement of quantitative details, restructuring of qualified intervals and coded value sets, and R6-only metadata/composition features that cannot round-trip to R4. Confidence is high for structural validation effects and medium for terminology/rationale details.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should be treated as a resource remodel rather than a simple version bump. R4 instances must gain a valid publication `status`; R4 quantitative details need a policy-driven transform to `permittedUnit` plus `permittedDataType=Quantity`; R4 qualified intervals need path renames and semantic review; and R4 top-level ValueSet references need conversion from `Reference(ValueSet)` to canonical URLs under `qualifiedValue`. R6-to-R4 conversion will often require extensions or lossy omission for canonical metadata, derivation, subject/performer/specimen/device/group/component fields, and context-specific qualified value sets.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high because the R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions and package index entries were present and directly compared. Confidence is lower for intended rationale, real-world prevalence, and external terminology consequences because official diffs, narrative pages, and terminology expansions were not supplied.

findings.title: R6 adds mandatory modifier status

oldState.summary: R4 ObservationDefinition had no local status element.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 `ObservationDefinition` could be valid with only the required `code` and no publication lifecycle status.

newState.summary: R6 requires ObservationDefinition.status 1..1 and marks it as a modifier.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local publication-status CodeSystem has the same four codes in R4 and R6, but the element itself is new on ObservationDefinition in R6.

semanticText.definition: The current state of the ObservationDefinition.
semanticText.comment: Unknown does not represent other; one of the defined statuses must apply.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 makes lifecycle status part of the resource contract and requires systems to interpret it because retired/unknown definitions can change safe use.

facts.note: The element did not exist in R4 and is mandatory in R6.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct R4-to-R6 validation break because R4 instances do not have `status` and R6 requires it. It is also a runtime risk for generated R6 classes and validators because `status` is a required modifier code that cannot be ignored safely.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Using an inactive or unknown definition as though it were active can affect ordering, catalog display, or interpretation policy.

justification.inferredGoal: Align ObservationDefinition with canonical definitional resources and make publication lifecycle explicit.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `status` as optional with missing meaning `unknown`, or use a transition warning before later requiring it.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Making lifecycle state explicit is a reasonable R6 goal for a definitional resource, especially because inactive or unknown definitions can affect safe use. The immediate `1..1` modifier requirement is a hard R4-to-R6 validation break, but a fully optional base element would not meet the same uniform lifecycle guarantee. The break therefore looks probably justified, with a real but incomplete less-breaking path.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have introduced `ObservationDefinition.status` as `0..1` with missing meaning `unknown` and a best-practice or warning invariant, then raised the base cardinality in a later release. That would preserve old R4 instances. The tradeoff is that base R6 consumers would have to handle absent status indefinitely, and profile-only requiredness would be migration mitigation rather than the same base-resource guarantee.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances but leaves lifecycle state absent or ambiguous on base R6 definitions and weakens uniform modifier handling.

evidence.detail: No R4 local element with id ObservationDefinition.status exists.
R6 defines status as 1..1 code with required publication-status binding and isModifier true.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment shows the minimal local issue: an R4 instance with the required `code` but no `status` needs an R6 publication status assigned.

findings.narrativeMd: `ObservationDefinition.status` is new and mandatory in R6. This is the clearest hard instance break because old R4 content has no native place for this value. Migration cannot be purely syntactic; an authoring or governance decision is needed to choose `draft`, `active`, `retired`, or `unknown`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid instance without `status` is invalid against the R6 StructureDefinition. R6 instances containing `status` are not natively representable in R4 because R4 has no element at that path, though an extension could preserve it.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Populate `status` during migration using catalog governance metadata where available. Avoid defaulting all records to `active` unless that is clinically and operationally justified; use `unknown` when the lifecycle state is genuinely not known. Add tests for missing status and each allowed status code.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is probably justified for a definitional artifact, but it is not wire-compatible. A staged optional-then-required path or profile requirement would have reduced immediate breakage.

findings.title: R6 adds canonical publication and derivation metadata not present in R4

oldState.summary: R4 had only `identifier` among this metadata group.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `ObservationDefinition` did not have canonical URL, version, name/title, publication metadata, use context, jurisdiction, copyright, review dates, effective period, or derivation elements.

newState.summary: R6 adds many optional metadata fields around canonical identity, publication, context, and derivation.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `url`, `version`, `versionAlgorithm[x]`, `name`, `title`, `experimental`, `date`, `publisher`, `contact`, `description`, `useContext`, `jurisdiction`, `purpose`, `copyright`, `copyrightLabel`, `approvalDate`, `lastReviewDate`, `effectivePeriod`, `derivedFromCanonical`, and `derivedFromUri`; most are summary elements.

facts.newValue: Many new metadata elements have isSummary=true.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances when moving forward to R6, but R6 instances using these fields cannot be represented as conformant R4 ObservationDefinition resources without extensions or data loss. Generated R4 models and strict parsers will reject these unknown elements.

justification.inferredGoal: Make ObservationDefinition behave like a publishable canonical definition artifact.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 compatibility alternative applies; the new publication and derivation metadata fields are optional additions.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The added canonical metadata supports governance, discovery, versioning, and derivation, and it does not invalidate R4 instances because the fields are optional. This finding is mainly an R6-to-R4 representability concern rather than a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The native R6 design is already forward-compatible for R4 instances: old resources can omit these optional fields. Carrying the same metadata in R4 extensions or sidecar records may help downgrade exchange, but that is a cross-version mitigation and should not be counted as a backward-compatible alternative to the R6 base model.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 downgrade remains lossy unless extensions are used, but extensions are mitigation, not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R4 local elements do not include canonical publication metadata other than identifier.
R6 adds optional metadata and derivation elements with local paths under ObservationDefinition.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 fragment uses standard fields that have no R4 paths. An R4 representation would need extensions or would drop them.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 turns `ObservationDefinition` into a richer publishable artifact. This is beneficial for catalogs and governance, but cross-version exchange is not lossless because R4 lacks the fields.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is not broken by optional additions. R6-to-R4 validation is affected whenever these elements are present because they are unknown in R4.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For forward migration, populate metadata where known, especially `url`, `version`, `name`, and review/effective dates. For downgrade, define explicit extensions or a sidecar catalog record for metadata that R4 cannot carry.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding optional fields is the least disruptive native R6 mechanism. Cross-version compatibility still requires extensions because R4 cannot be changed retroactively.

findings.title: R4 quantitativeDetails backbone is removed and partially replaced by permittedUnit

oldState.summary: R4 had an optional quantitativeDetails backbone with customaryUnit, unit, conversionFactor, and decimalPrecision.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could describe one SI unit, one customary unit, a conversion factor between them, and decimal precision for quantitative results.

newState.summary: R6 removes quantitativeDetails and adds repeated permittedUnit Coding.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 represents allowed Quantity units as repeated `permittedUnit` codings. It has no direct local replacement for R4 `customaryUnit`, `conversionFactor`, or `decimalPrecision`.

facts.oldValue: CodeableConcept for unit/customaryUnit plus decimal/integer details

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `permittedUnit` maps to the same V2 mapping as the old SI unit and has a UCUM units binding, but it does not preserve the full old quantitativeDetails backbone.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance containing `quantitativeDetails` is invalid against R6 because the element no longer exists. A syntactic transform can map simple units to `permittedUnit`, but conversion factor, precision, and SI/customary distinctions are not natively preserved.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Unit and precision metadata can affect result validation, rounding, and display in laboratory catalogs.

justification.inferredGoal: Simplify quantitative unit modeling and allow multiple permitted units.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated `quantitativeDetails` alongside `permittedUnit`, or keep explicit unit, precision, and conversion fields while adding a repeatable unit list.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of simplifying allowed-unit modeling and supporting multiple permitted units is reasonable, but removing `quantitativeDetails` makes R4 instances invalid and can lose decimal precision, conversion factor, and SI/customary distinctions. A less-breaking design exists, but it would keep an old backbone with semantics that overlap the new model and might be inconsistently maintained. That makes the breaking cleanup probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have kept `quantitativeDetails` as a deprecated base element while adding `permittedUnit`, or could have retained native replacement fields for `customaryUnit`, `conversionFactor`, and `decimalPrecision`. This would preserve more R4 data. The material tradeoff is duplicate same-resource unit representations: deprecated `quantitativeDetails.unit` and new `permittedUnit` could conflict, validators would need reconciliation rules, and the older representation might persist indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances but creates overlapping unit representations and ambiguity around precision, conversion, and preferred-vs-permitted unit semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 defines quantitativeDetails 0..1 BackboneElement.
R4 defines customaryUnit, unit, conversionFactor, and decimalPrecision under quantitativeDetails.
R6 defines permittedUnit 0..* Coding with preferred UCUM binding and no quantitativeDetails element.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example preserves a simple UCUM unit but drops `decimalPrecision`; local extensions or catalog metadata would be needed for lossless preservation.

findings.narrativeMd: `quantitativeDetails` is not just renamed. R6 replaces the unit part with `permittedUnit` and drops native fields that expressed customary-vs-SI unit, conversion factor, and decimal precision. Existing R4 clients and generated models that read those paths will fail or silently lose information unless a migration rule is added.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `quantitativeDetails` are old-valid/new-invalid. R6 instances with multiple `permittedUnit` values are not cleanly representable in R4 because R4 has at most one `unit` and one `customaryUnit`, plus no generic permitted-unit list.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map simple `quantitativeDetails.unit.coding` and possibly `customaryUnit.coding` to `permittedUnit`. Add `permittedDataType=Quantity` when any `permittedUnit` is present. Preserve conversion factor and decimal precision in extensions, implementation-guide rules, or an external catalog if they are operationally important.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible R6 design could have kept the old backbone as deprecated and introduced `permittedUnit` for the new use case. The current design is simpler but forces migration and can be lossy.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is needed for catalogs where decimal precision or conversion factor drives validation or display.

findings.title: R6 adds invariant requiring Quantity when permittedUnit is present

oldState.summary: R4 had no local invariant tying quantitative unit metadata to permittedDataType.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 instance could include `quantitativeDetails.unit` without also declaring `permittedDataType` containing `Quantity`.

newState.summary: R6 invariant obd-0 requires permittedDataType to contain Quantity when permittedUnit exists.

constraints.human: If permittedUnit exists, then permittedDataType=Quantity must exist.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 validates consistency between units and allowed value datatypes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The invariant applies to a new R6 element, so an untouched R4 instance will already fail for removed paths or missing status before this rule matters. However, a direct migration that maps R4 unit metadata to `permittedUnit` without adding `permittedDataType=Quantity` will fail R6 validation.

justification.inferredGoal: Prevent unit declarations when Quantity results are not allowed.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Use a warning or best-practice invariant during transition instead of an error-level rule.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The invariant is logically consistent: declaring permitted units only makes sense when Quantity results are permitted. It is not a direct break for untouched R4 wire content because `permittedUnit` is new, but it can break naive migrations from old unit metadata. A softer rule would be less disruptive for transformed content, yet would materially weaken R6 validation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design would make `obd-0` warning-level or transitional instead of an error. That is only a partial alternative because correct migrations can add `permittedDataType=Quantity`, while genuinely inconsistent R6 resources should be rejected rather than normalized silently.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: A warning eases automated migration but allows R6 instances where units imply Quantity while `permittedDataType` omits it.

evidence.detail: R6 defines an error invariant requiring Quantity in permittedDataType when permittedUnit exists.
No corresponding R4 local invariant is present.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 migration must add `Quantity`; otherwise `permittedUnit` violates `obd-0`.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a local consistency rule that can surprise automated transformations. Mapping a unit is not enough; the migrated definition must also say Quantity is an allowed result type.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is a potential old-valid/new-invalid pattern for migrated content rather than for untouched R4 wire content. It affects validators and generated test fixtures that create `permittedUnit` but omit `permittedDataType`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Whenever a migration populates `ObservationDefinition.permittedUnit`, ensure `permittedDataType` contains `Quantity`. If the old record explicitly excluded Quantity, flag it for manual review instead of generating an inconsistent R6 resource.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The invariant is clinically and logically sensible. A softer transition could have used a warning, but the new element gives implementers a clear validation rule.

findings.title: qualifiedInterval is replaced by qualifiedValue with renamed children and broader semantics

oldState.summary: R4 had qualifiedInterval 0..* for ranges, with category, range, context, appliesTo, gender, age, gestationalAge, and condition.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled qualified ranges for continuous and ordinal observation results.

newState.summary: R6 has qualifiedValue 0..* for ranges and coded value sets, with rangeCategory and sexParameterForClinicalUse replacing category and gender.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 broadens the backbone from intervals to qualified values, keeping context/appliesTo/age/gestationalAge/condition/range concepts but changing paths and terminology.

facts.oldValue: Qualified range for continuous and ordinal results
facts.newValue: Set of qualified values, including ranges and qualitative value sets

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The cardinalities and several child paths align directly, while R6 changes the backbone name and expands the scope beyond ranges.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances containing `qualifiedInterval` use element names that do not exist in R6. R6 instances use new element names and can express non-range qualified value sets that R4 cannot model under `qualifiedInterval`.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Reference ranges and population qualifiers can affect interpretation of abnormal, critical, or applicable results.

justification.inferredGoal: Generalize qualified result constraints beyond interval ranges.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 `qualifiedInterval` path and broaden its definition and children to cover qualified values.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Generalizing interval ranges into qualified values is a reasonable goal, but the wire-path rename from `qualifiedInterval` to `qualifiedValue` appears more breaking than necessary. Living with the older name while clarifying the definition and adding the new coded-value capabilities would preserve most R4 instances with modest long-term cost.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would retain `ObservationDefinition.qualifiedInterval` as the native backbone, keep its existing children valid, rename only definitions and short text, and add the R6 qualitative value-set children there. Keeping both old and new backbones would introduce duplicate representations, but simply broadening the old path would meet the core R6 goal without invalidating old instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances with a nonoptimal name and some semantic awkwardness, but avoids duplicate representations if the old path is broadened rather than paralleled.

evidence.detail: R4 defines qualifiedInterval 0..* BackboneElement.
R6 defines qualifiedValue 0..* BackboneElement.
R6 replaces the old gender path with sexParameterForClinicalUse while retaining a required administrative-gender value set binding.

examples.examplesMd: The example illustrates the mechanical path changes. Local policy should confirm whether old `gender` values should always map to R6 `sexParameterForClinicalUse`.

findings.narrativeMd: `qualifiedInterval` is replaced by `qualifiedValue`. The common range fields are still recognizable, but their JSON paths changed and the backbone now also hosts qualitative coded value-set constraints. This affects validators, serializers, FHIRPath expressions, generated classes, and any catalog logic that reads reference ranges.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `qualifiedInterval` is invalid in R6. An R6 instance with `qualifiedValue` is invalid in R4 unless transformed back, and not all R6 qualified-value content has an R4 equivalent.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `qualifiedInterval` to `qualifiedValue`, `category` to `rangeCategory`, and `gender` to `sexParameterForClinicalUse`; carry context, appliesTo, age, gestationalAge, condition, and range across. Review the gender-to-sex-parameter semantic change and add tests for range-only and value-set-bearing qualified values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broader R6 model is understandable, but retaining a deprecated `qualifiedInterval` path or adding aliases would have made old instances easier to validate and transform.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 field name `sexParameterForClinicalUse` is semantically different from R4 `gender`, but its required binding remains administrative-gender in the supplied StructureDefinition.

findings.title: Coded value set references move under qualifiedValue and change from Reference to canonical

oldState.summary: R4 had top-level valid/normal/abnormal/critical coded value set elements, each 0..1 Reference(ValueSet).
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 represented global coded-result value sets using Reference elements at the resource root.

newState.summary: R6 places valid/normal/abnormal/critical coded value set elements inside qualifiedValue, each 0..1 canonical(ValueSet).
newState.narrativeMd: R6 represents coded-result value sets as canonical URLs scoped to a qualified-value context.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Names and definitions match closely, but the elements moved under `qualifiedValue` and the serialization type changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a hard path and type change. R4 Reference objects are not valid at the old top-level paths in R6, and R6 canonical strings under repeated qualified values cannot always be represented by the single top-level R4 Reference fields.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Valid, normal, abnormal, and critical coded-result sets can influence validation and interpretation of qualitative observations.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow value sets to vary by qualified context and use canonical references for definitional artifacts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep deprecated top-level `Reference(ValueSet)` fields for unqualified global value sets while adding contextual canonical fields under `qualifiedValue`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Context-scoped value sets and canonical references are reasonable R6 goals for definitional content. A less-breaking path could preserve common unqualified R4 value-set references, but it would not cover the full contextual model and would create parallel places to say the same thing. The current break is therefore probably justified, with a partial alternative for common cases.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have retained `validCodedValueSet`, `normalCodedValueSet`, `abnormalCodedValueSet`, and `criticalCodedValueSet` at the resource root as deprecated aliases for global value sets, while adding the new `qualifiedValue.*CodedValueSet` canonical fields for context-specific values. This preserves old instances in the simple case. The tradeoff is persistent duplicate same-resource representations and ambiguity when both the old global Reference and the new unqualified canonical are populated.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Covers common global R4 cases but duplicates the same fact, leaves Reference-vs-canonical ambiguity, and cannot express multiple context-specific R6 value sets in the old shape.

evidence.detail: R4 defines top-level validCodedValueSet 0..1 Reference(ValueSet); the normal, abnormal, and critical variants follow the same pattern.
R6 defines qualifiedValue.validCodedValueSet 0..1 canonical(ValueSet); the normal, abnormal, and critical variants follow the same pattern.

examples.examplesMd: The old Reference may contain relative references, display text, identifiers, or contained-resource assumptions. R6 canonical requires a canonical URL string.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 global coded value-set references become R6 context-scoped canonical URLs. This changes both where the data lives and how it is serialized. It also changes the expressive model: R6 can attach different value sets to different qualified contexts.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with top-level coded value set elements are invalid in R6. R6 instances with multiple context-specific value sets cannot be represented faithfully in R4, which has only one global element of each category.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Convert each R4 ValueSet Reference to a canonical URL where possible and place it in a `qualifiedValue` occurrence. If the R4 reference is relative or points to a contained ValueSet, resolve or mint a canonical URL. Preserve display/identifier information in extensions or local catalog metadata if needed.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 approach is more canonical and context-aware, but a transitional global element would have made the common unqualified case easier to migrate.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Manual review is needed when R4 references are not canonical URLs or when multiple R6 qualified values must be downgraded to R4.

findings.title: R6 adds subject, performer, body structure, specimen, device, group, and component modeling

oldState.summary: R4 had no local fields for subject type, performer type, body structure, specimen definition, device, group membership, or components.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 ObservationDefinition was comparatively flat and did not model panels/components or specimen/device context directly.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional fields for observation subject, performer, body structure, specimen, device, hasMember, and component definitions.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `subject`, `performerType`, `bodyStructure`, `specimen`, `device[x]`, `hasMember`, and repeated `component` with component code, permitted data type, unit, and qualified values.

facts.newValue: component obd-1 requires permittedDataType=Quantity when component.permittedUnit exists.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These additions do not invalidate R4 instances, but R6 instances using them cannot be represented natively in R4. They also create generated-code and serializer changes because R6 includes a new choice element and a recursive contentReference for component qualified values.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Specimen, body structure, device, and component definitions can affect whether the definition is applicable to an ordered or resulted observation.

justification.inferredGoal: Support richer definition of observation panels, components, devices, specimens, and applicability context.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 breaking alternative applies; subject, performer, body structure, specimen, device, group, and component fields are optional R6 additions.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The new fields fill real modeling gaps for panels, components, devices, specimens, and applicability context, and they do not invalidate R4 instances because they are optional. The compatibility concern is chiefly that R6 instances using the new model cannot be downgraded losslessly to R4.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed for forward compatibility: old R4 instances can simply omit the optional fields. R4 extensions or external catalog records can preserve these concepts for downgrade exchange, but those are mitigation strategies rather than alternatives to the R6 base resource shape.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 exchange may need extensions or data loss, but that is downgrade mitigation rather than a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R6 adds subject 0..* CodeableConcept.
R6 adds device[x] with Reference(Device) and canonical(DeviceDefinition) choices.
R6 adds component 0..* with required component.code and child content.

examples.examplesMd: R4 has no `hasMember` or `component` paths on ObservationDefinition, so a downgrade would require extensions or separate resources.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds substantial new modeling for what an observation definition applies to and how grouped/component observations are defined. This is mostly a round-trip and runtime issue rather than an R4-to-R6 validation issue.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances remain valid with respect to these optional additions. R6 instances using these fields are not R4-representable without extensions, and generated code must handle `device[x]` and `component.qualifiedValue` contentReference correctly.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For forward migration, populate these fields only when trustworthy source catalog data exists. For downgrade, define a loss policy: drop, extension-map, or split into external catalog records. Include tests for component code being mandatory inside each R6 component and for `obd-1` when component permitted units are present.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the fields are optional, R6 did not break old instances to add this expressiveness. Backward compatibility with R4 exchange still depends on extensions because R4 cannot natively carry the model.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The local impact is high for systems that need R6-to-R4 downgrade or single code models generated from both versions.

findings.title: code example binding changes from all observation codes to observation-or-both LOINC subset

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 compose includes all LOINC codes via system http://loinc.org.
R6 compose includes LOINC codes where ORDER_OBS is Observation or Both. No expansion was available to enumerate affected codes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The binding strength remains `example`, so this should not make existing codes structurally invalid. It can still affect terminology pick lists, conformance guidance, code generation of example bindings, and business rules that treat the example value set as preferred.

findings.narrativeMd: The required `code` element remains 1..1 CodeableConcept, but its example binding points to a narrower LOINC-oriented value set in R6. findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is not a hard validation break under base FHIR binding rules. It is a semantic/conformance risk for systems that over-enforce example bindings or use them to generate enumerations or pick lists.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not auto-reject existing R4 codes solely because the example value set changed. Use a terminology service to identify LOINC codes outside the R6 example set if local policy wants to align with the new guidance.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the binding remains example strength, the change is mostly backward-compatible. A narrative-only recommendation would have had even less tooling impact but less computable guidance.
